correctness.rationale: For every N>=4 and 0<=j<=N-3 a j-face is precisely a crossed (j+1)-face of the N-vertex simplex, giving the exact binomial sign-count formula. Gaussian projection onto sum-zero normals gives Haar measure. The centered empirical-threshold count has iid influence summands with variance 1/4-1/(2pi); a grid/Bernstein argument controls the moving threshold. Symmetric binomial Taylor expansion gives the normalized quadratic deficits at every fixed j. DKW and Gaussian concentration uniformly bound all sign-imbalance moments, legitimizing polynomial joint moment convergence and the covariance constant 2s^4/(2^(j+k)j!k!). Pair-Gaussian quadrants give the exact vertex mean; the deficit is at most the squared imbalance and gives the concentration inequality. Geometric hull constructions for 125 sections and 195000 Gaussian normals provide finite checks only. No unproved growing-rank or independent certification is claimed.

originality.rationale: The compared primary literature treats section volumes and extremal sections (Dirksen), expected face counts of projected regular polytopes (Affentranger–Schneider; Kabluchko–Thäle), and expected high-dimensional Gaussian-polytope facets (Böröczky–Lugosi–Reitzner). Projection distributional equivalence (Baryshnikov–Vitale) does not itself imply the distribution of centroidal-section face vectors. The Gaussian statistical threshold count is a known type of observable and is not independently claimed. No identified inspected source states the full exact common-imbalance section f-vector plus nonGaussian chi-square joint deficit/covariance theorem. Absence of an equivalent indexed source is not absolute priority proof; inaccessible historical full texts remain risks.
residual_risks: Full texts of the 1992 and 1994 projection papers were not available, so unknown historical reductions cannot be excluded.
A known result in empirical-process theory may imply the Gaussian sign-imbalance CLT; novelty is not claimed for that lemma in isolation.
Broad mathematical database searches do not prove uniqueness or exclude unindexed earlier central-section results.

value.rationale: A regular simplex is the natural maximally symmetric finite polytope, and a uniformly oriented centroidal hyperplane yields a canonical random section. Its entire f-vector has only one random parameter, which yields a common, nonGaussian chi-square limit at every fixed rank. Sharp exponents/constants for covariances and perfect asymptotic cross-rank correlation measure combinatorial complexity fluctuations in a way not captured by known expected f-vectors or volume extremizers. The exact reductions and joint laws form a useful self-contained benchmark for broader random-section geometry.
